Ores and Raw Materials Sectional Committee, MTD 13

FOREWORD This Indian Standard (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Ores and Raw Materials Sectional Committee had been approved by the Metallurgical Engineering Division Council. This standard was originally published in 1961 and revised in 1976. Since then, a lot of developments have taken place in manganese ore industry and trade. In this standard, sampling procedures for ROM and sized ores have been covered. With typical export consignments being around 15 000-20 000 MT, the sampling procedure covers all types of ores and accounts for optimum sizes of gross samples. This standard is also applicable for the sampling of ferruginous manganese ores, manganeferous iron ores, manganese ore concentrates and other superior grades, such as, manganese dioxide ores and chemical grade ores. However, manganeferous iron ores containing less than 10 percent manganese do not come under the perview of this standard. This standard mainly deals with manual sampling of manganese ores and such cannot be employed in those cases where sampling and sample preparation are fully mechanized. In the formulation of this standard due consideration has been given to international co-ordination among the standards and practice prevailing in different countries. For this purpose, reference has been made to the following documents issued by the International Organization for Standardization: ISO 4296-1 Manganese ores -- Sampling -- Part 1: Increment sampling ISO 4296-2 Manganese ores -- Sampling -- Part 2: Preparation of samples For the determination of size distribution of manganese ores, sieve conforming to IS 460 (Part 1) : 1985 `Specification for test sieves: Part 1 Wire cloth test sieves (third revision)' and IS 460 (Part 2) : 1985 `Specification for test sieves : Part 2 Perforated plate sieves (third revision )' shall be used. When such sieves are not available, other equivalent standard sieves as judged by the aperture size may be used. In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value observed or calculated is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)'.

IS 1449 : 2010

Indian Standard METHODS OF SAMPLING OF MANGANESE ORES ( Second Revision )
1 SCOPE This standard prescribes the procedure for collection and preparation of samples of manganese ores from wagons, trucks, ships, and stockpiles for the determination of size distribution, moisture content, chemical composition of the ore in the lot. It also lays down a method for reporting the quality of material sampled. The samples should be drawn keeping in mind that separate samples should be drawn for each type/category/source of ore since otherwise the representativeness of the sample may not be maintained. 2 REFERENCES The standards listed below contain provisions, which though reference in this text, constitute, provisions of this standard. At the time of publication, the editions indicated were valid. All standards are subject to revision, and parties to aggreements based on this standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent editions of the standards listed below: Title Specification for test sieves: Wire cloth test sieves ( third revision ) (Part 2) : 1985 Perforated plate test sieves (third revision ) 1548 (Part 1) : 1981 Manual on basic principles of lot sampling (second revision) 4905 : 1968 Methods for random sampling 11153 : 1996 Manganese dioxide for dry batteries � Specification ( first revision ) 3 TERMINOLOGY For the purpose of this standard, the following definitions shall apply. 3.1 Run-of-Mine Ore -- Run-of-mine ores consisting of all sizes up to 200 mm. 3.2 Sized Ore -- Ores of size greater than 6 mm but not exceeding 75 mm. 3.3 Fines -- Ores with maximum particle size 6 mm. IS No. 460 (Part 1) : 1985 3.4 Lot -- The quantity of ore indicated to be the same category ( see 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3) and offered for inspection at one time. A lot may consist of the whole or a part of the quantity ordered for. 3.5 Sub-lot -- The quantity of ore in each of the parts into which a lot is divided for the purpose of sampling. 3.6 Increment -- The quantity of ore obtained by a sampling device at one time from a lot or sub-lot. 3.7 Unit Sample -- The quantity of ore collected at one point in sectional sampling or at one time from the conveyer by stopped belt method. 3.8 Gross Sample -- Sample as collected from a sublot, that is, the quantity of ore consisting of one or several increments or unit samples taken from a sublot. 3.9 Size Sample -- The sample taken for the determination of the size distribution of the lot or sub-lot. 3.10 Laboratory Sample (Sub-lot) -- The quantity of ore obtained by reducing a gross sample following a specified procedure and intended for laboratory testing. 3.11 Moisture Sample -- The sample to be used exclusively for the purpose of determining moisture content. 3.12 Composite Sample for the Lot -- The quantity of ore obtained by mixing together equal quantities of the ore, at appropriate stage of sample preparation from each of the sub-lot laboratory sample or physical test sample. When sub-lots vary in mass, quantities of laboratory samples or physical test samples proportionate to the sample or the sub-lot may be taken and mixed together.
NOTE -- Whenever preparation of sub-lot laboratory samples is not required, the composite sample for the lot can be prepared by mixing gross samples �10 mm stage in proporation to sub-lot tonnages.

3.13 Manual Sampling -- The collection of sample increments by human effort. 3.14 Maximum Particle Size -- Particle size expressed in terms of the size aperture of the sieve 1

IS 1449 : 2010 on which approximately 5 percent in mass of the ore is retained. 3.15 Whole Through Sieve Size -- The size of the smallest aperture through which all of the sample passes. 3.16 Almost Uniform Mass -- The co-efficient of variation of increment masses shall not exceed 20 percent. 4 GENERAL PROCEDURE FOR SAMPLING 4.1 Sub-lots For the purpose of sampling, a lot shall be divided into a number of the sub-lots of approximately equal mass as specified in Table 1. However, it is very important that the sub-lot be comprised of only a single category or type of ore. Considering that typically, consignments of manganese ore consist of heterogeneous ore, care should be taken to draw separate samples from each category or source of ore to ensure representativeness of the sample drawn.
NOTE -- When it is not practicable to have sub-lots or approximately equal mass, sub-lots which varying mass may also be permitted.

been taken, increments shall be continue to be taken at the same interval until the completion of handling.
NOTE � When the mass of the gross sample is expected to be less than that required quantity for the tests, the number of increments shall be increased.

4.1.3 Sampling should be carried out at the nearest possible location to the loading or discharging facilities, preferably immediately before or immediately after the point of weighing. Free fall drops during handling of sized ore samples shall be kept to a minimum to reduce size degradation of the ore. 4.2 Minimum Mass and Number of Increments The mass of the increment to be taken from a sub-lot for drawing the gross sample shall be governed by the maximum particle size of the ore to be sampled. The number of increment to be taken from a sub-lot for drawing the gross sample shall be governed by the mass of the gross sample and the mass of the increments as specified in Table 2 for various categories of ores as specified by their maximum particle sizes. This number shall be evenly distributed over the sub-lot. The increments of almost uniform mass shall be drawn with suitable sampling scoop (see Fig.1) at regular intervals. 5 SAMPLING FROM CONVEYORS BY STOPPED- BELT METHOD 5.1 When manganese ore is moved on conveyors, one of the most reliable methods of manual sampling is the stopped-belt method. Whenever, it is practicable to stop the conveyer belt periodically, a large quantity of ore known as unit sample may be drawn by stopping the belt. However, it should be noted that if possible, the samples should be drawn from the conveyor depending upon the category or nature of the ore and that lots shall be constituted of the same category or source of the ore. The mass of different unit samples shall not be less than that given below and shall be collected from the full width and thickness of the ores stream over a suitable length of the conveyor. The number of unit samples to be drawn at regular interval to constitute a gross sample shall be as given in Table 3 for different categories of manganese ores and should be evenly distributed over the sub-lot. 5.2 In case it is not possible to stop the conveyor, increments according to Table 2 shall be collected at regular intervals at a suitable transfer point in the conveyor system. It is recommended that sample increments should be taken at a place where it is possible to cut across the entire falling stream of material by means of a suitable receptacle passing from one side of the stream to the other without allowing the receptacle to overflow. Stopped-belt conveyor sampling using a sampling frame is given in Annex A. 2

4.1.1 A representative gross sample shall be drawn from each of the sub-lots and shall be kept separately. There will be as many gross samples as number of sub-lots. The sample shall be preserved in water-proof containers and closed with suitable lids, as soon as they are drawn. The containers shall not be exposed to heat thereafter. 4.1.2 Sampling shall be carried out, preferably, during shifting of a lot at the time of its delivery. The sampling shall be carried out by the method of periodic systematic sampling meaning thereby that each increment shall be taken at a specific regular interval in terms of mass thoughout the whole mass of the lot and shall not be changed in the course of sampling. 5.3 The material collected as unit samples or increments in a sub-lot shall be aggregated and mixed together to constitute a gross sample. 6 SAMPLING DURING LOADING AND UNLOADING OF WAGONS 6.1 Sub-lots For the purpose of sampling, all the wagons in a lot 3

shall be divided into a suitable number of sub-lots of approximately equal mass in accordance with the requirements of Table 1. 6.1.1 A representative gross sample shall be drawn from each of the sub-lots and shall be kept separately. Thus, there will be as many gross samples as the number of sub-lots into which a lot has been divided. Where different grades ore are being loaded/

IS 1449 : 2010 unloaded into/from wagons each grade will be covered under at least one sub-lot. Where different grades ore are being loaded/unloaded into/from wagons each grade will be covered under at least one sub-lot. 6.2 In order to get a representative gross sample, the ore shall be sampled as far as possible, in a steady motion during loading or unloading of the wagon. 6.2.1 A 100 percent of the wagons shall be sampled at random from the sub-lot. The number of increments to be taken from the selected wagons and the mass of the increments and the gross sample shall be in accordance with Table 2. The increments shall be evenly distributed over the wagon with the view to determining the necessary number of increments that should be collected from each of the wagons of the sub-lots for making of the gross sample. These increments shall be drawn with the help of a suitable scoop (see Fig.1) at regular intervals at the time of loading or unloading of the wagons.
NOTES 1 While taking the increments as described above, if a large lump is encountered at any point and cannot be taken in the scoop, it shall be picked up as such. The lump so obtained shall, however, be accounted for in the determination of the ore size distribution as given under 10 and in the reduction of gross samples as given under 11. 2 If agreed to 50 percent of the wagons may be selected, at random from the sub-lot, for sampling by the given method.

7.2 In order to get representative sample, increments shall be drawn at the time of loading or unloading of the trucks. From each truck in the sub-lot, a minimum of one increment shall be drawn. For drawing increments 8 kg or 4 kg sampling scoop (see Fig.1) shall be used depending on the category of the ore. At the time of taking increments care shall be taken not to exclude deliberately lumps or fines and this will be ensured by drawing increments in the middle of loading/unloading time of a truck. 7.3 The aggregate of material collected from the various increments or unit samples from a sub-lot shall constitute a gross sample. 8 SAMPLING FROM SHIPS CONTAINERS AND BARGES DURING LOADING/UNLOADING 8.1 For the purpose of sampling the quantity of ore to be loaded into or unloaded from ship and barges shall be divided into a suitable number of sub-lot of approximately equal mass in accordance with Table 1. 8.2 In order to get representative gross sample, ore shall be sampled as far as possible when in motion. If it is taken on a conveyor, the gross sample shall be collected according to the procedure laid down in 5. If the ore is handled in any other manner the gross samples may be drawn loading or unloading of the ship. For this purpose, the number of increment to be taken at regular intervals and the mass of the increments and gross sample shall be in accordance with Table 2 for different categories of ore (see 6.2.1) and Table 3 for container sampling. 8.3 The aggregate of the material collected from the various increments or units samples from a sub-lot shall constitute a gross sample.
NOTE -- Sampling from a loaded ship should always be avoided.

7 SAMPLING DURING LOADING OR UNLOADING OF TRUCKS 7.1 Sub-lot Quite often the nature of manganese ore tendered in trucks is as heterogeneous as that supplied in wagons or ships and variations in terms of particle size and chemical composition has been found to be considerable which requires limiting of sub-lot tonnage. Hence, when manganese ore is supplied in trucks the sub-lot size shall not exceed 50 trucks counted on continuous basis. If loading or unloading is done shift-wise, sub-lots may be conveniently formed in terms of trucks handled in one shift, subject to the condition that the size of each sub-lot shall not exceed 50 trucks. 100 percent of the trucks are to be sampled irrespective of whether the ores originate from a single source or more than one source. The number of increments per truck shall be adjusted so that total number of increments from each sub-lot (50 trucks or less) is always greater than or equal to the number specified in Table 2 for various categories of ores. However, it is recommended that separate samples be drawn for each category/source of ore. 4

8.4 Container Sampling Normally natural manganese dioxide ore of 72 percent MnO 2 and above is used for dry batteries and chemical industry. It is partly imported and partly mined indigenously. The mixed ore is sized to about 30 mm and less and then ground to pass 100 micron size or less. This ground material is packed into containers, such as, HDPE woven bags protected by polyethylene lining inside and then sold to the end user. The sampling method specified under this clause is called container sampling. 8.4.1 General Requirements of Sampling In drawing, preparing, storing and handling test sample, the following precautions and directions shall be observed. 8.4.1.1 Sample shall not be drawn in an exposed place.

IS 1449 : 2010 8.4.1.2 Precautions shall be taken to protect the samples, the material being sampled and the sampling instrument from adventitious contamination. 8.4.1.3 To draw a representative sample, the contents of each container selected for sampling shall be mixed thoroughly by suitable means. 8.4.1.4 The sampled material shall be placed in clean, dry, air-tight glass or other suitable containers which have no action on the material. 8.4.1.5 Each sample container shall be sealed airtight with a stopper after filling and shall be marked with all particulars of the material and date of sampling. 8.4.2 Scale of Sampling 8.4.2.1 Lot In a single consignment of the material all the containers of the same type and the size and drawn from the same batch of manufacture shall constitute a lot. If a consignment is known to consist of different batches of manufacture or of different types and sizes of containers, the containers belonging to the same batch, type and size shall be grouped together and each such group shall constitute a separate lot. 8.4.2.2 For ascertaining the conformity of the material in a lot to the requirements of the specification, tests shall be carried out for each lot separately. The number of containers to be selected at random from lots of different sizes shall be in accordance with Table 4. Table 4 Scale of Sampling
Sl No. Number of Containers in the Lot N (2) Up to 25 26-50 51-100 101 and above Minimum Number of Sublots into which a Lot is Divided n (3) 3 4 5 7

Arrange the containers in the lot in a systematic order and starting from any one count them as 1, 2, 3...., etc, up to r and so on where r is the integral part of N/n (N and n being the lot size and sample size respectively). Every rth container thus counted shall be withdrawn to constitute the sample. 8.4.3 Preparation of Test Samples 8.4.3.1 From each of the containers selected, draw a representative sample increment of 250 g in mass. 8.4.3.2 Each sub-lot sample shall be thoroughly mixed to obtain a gross sample and reduced to prepare a composite sample of the lot of about 150 g. The composite sample shall be divided into three equal parts, one for the purchaser, another for the supplier, and the third to be used as a referee sample. 8.4.3.3 Divide the remaining portions of each lot to obtain a sample of about 200 g. Divide it into three equal parts and transfer the material to three separate bottles giving full identification particulars of the sample on the bottles. The material in each bottle constitute an individual sample. One of these three sets (each set containing a bottle representing n containers sampled) shall be for the purchaser, one for the supplier and the third for the referee. 8.4.4 Number of Tests 8.4.4.1 Tests for the determination of moisture content and manganese dioxide content shall be performed on each of the individual sample. 8.4.4.2 Tests for the determination of the remaining characterististics given in Table 1 shall be carried out on the composite sample. 8.4.5 Criteria for Conformity 8.4.5.1 For individual samples From each set of individual tests results moisture content and manganese dioxide content, respective average (X) and the range (R) of test results shall be computed (range R being defined as the difference between the maximum and the minimum values of test results) and the conditions specified in col 6 of Table 5 shall be satisfied (see IS 11153). 8.4.5.2 For composite samples For declaring the conformity of the lot to the

IS 1449 : 2010 requirements of all other characteristics tested on the composite sample, the test results shall meet the corresponding values specified in the Table 5. 9 SAMPLING FROM STOCKPILES 9.1 Sub-lots For the purpose of sampling, the quantity of manganese ore in a stockpile shall be divided into a suitable number of sub-lots of approximately equal mass or specified in Table 1. 9.1.1 A representative gross sample shall be drawn from each of the sub-lots and shall be kept separately. Thus, there will be as many gross samples as the number of sub-lots into which the lot has been divided. 9.2 Sampling of ore from stockpiles shall be carried out, as far as possible when ore is in motion, that is, during the making or breaking of the stockpiles. 9.2.1 The number of increments to be taken from a sublot for making up the gross sample shall be governed by the mass of gross sample and the mass of the increments as specified in Table 2 for various categories of manganese ore. This number shall be equally distributed over the sub-lot. The increment shall be drawn with the help of a suitable sampling scoop (see Fig.1) at regular intervals in the course of making or unmaking of the stockpiles (see also Notes 1 and 2 under 6.2.1). 9.3 When it becomes necessary to sample a stationary stockpiles, sectional sampling (see 9.3.1) and trench sampling method (see 9.3.2) may be used for a stockpiles up to a maximum height of 1.5 m only. In the former case, the requisite number of points shall be located at random on the entire surface of the sub-lots. The walking space at the ground level in the case must be kept at 0.3 m. In certain cases, due to practical constraints of space, material is stacked higher than 1.5 m, sometimes up to 3 m. in these cases, it may be required to sample such high stockpiles. Care must be taken to dig proper trench when sampling stacks of about 3 m height to ensure that the sample can be drawn from the exposed surfaces. 9.3.1 Sectional Sampling By this method, at least 5 unit samples in the case of fine ores and 10 unit samples in the case of sized ore are to be collected from each sub-lot. For this purpose, the requisite number of points shall be chosen at random on the entire surface of the stockpile. At each of the selected point, a circle of suitable diameter (minimum three times the largest particle size) shall be marked. The material over the area of this circle and along entire height of the stockpile from top to bottom shall be collected in stages. This can be carried out by taking ore up to a depth of 50 cm and covering the hole so formed by a plate for removing the ores lying on the sides of the hole. Then after removing the plate further 6 depth can be reached in the same manner and the ore can be collected from the freshly formed hole. 9.3.2 Trench Sampling The gross sample shall be made up of the number of increments as specified in Table 2. These increments shall be collected as indicated in 9.3.2.1. 9.3.2.1 Along a randomly chosen line on the ore surface of the sub-lot, a trench shall be dug, right down to the ground level leaving about 0.3 m walking space at the ground level (at least 0.5 m if the height of the stack is more than 1.5 m). From the trenches so dug, the required number of increment shall be collected with the help of a suitable sampling scoop, at various point randomly spread over the two exposed sides of the trenches. In case of large stockpiles, in addition to the trench, the sides of the piles may also be opened to expose the ore down to the bottom, at places where the trench does not expose the ore inside. For large stacks of about 3 m in height, at least 0.5 m of walking space should be kept at ground level. 10 DETERMINATION OF SIZE DISTRIBUTION 10.1 In the determination of ore size distribution, IS sieves of suitable sizes specified in IS 460 (Part 1) and IS 460 (Part 2) shall be used. The sieves which are to be used would depend upon the contractual requirements of the buyer and the seller. 10.2 Gross Sample Obtained from Aggregating Unit Samples Each gross sample shall be screened through selected IS sieves and the ore retained on each of the sieves and that passing through the smallest sieve shall be weighed separately. Ore size distribution of the lot shall be estimated as follows: Percentage mass in the size range `A'= a1 + a2 + an � 100 w1 + w2 + wn

where w1, w2 .....wn= mass of the different gross sample; and a1, a2........an= corresponding masses of ore in the size range `A' (A may be below, above, or bounded by two nominal sizes of IS sieves). 10.3 Gross Sample Obtained by Aggregating Increments 10.3.1 Where gross samples do not contain any lumps, the procedure detailed in 10.2 shall be followed for estimating the ore size distribution in the lot.

IS 1449 : 2010 10.3.2 Where the gross samples contain some lumps (see Notes 1 and 2 under 6.2.1 ) the portion of the gross samples excluding the lumps shall be treated as in 10.2 . 10.3.2.1 The ore size distribution of the lot shall be estimated as follows: a) Over 200 mm, n�8 percent = (n � 8) + w1 + w2 + w3....+wn b) Any other size fraction B = where b1 + b2 + b3 +.....+bn (n � 8) + w1 + w2 + w3...+wn drawn they shall be crushed to pass 10 mm IS sieve and further processed as detailed in Annex B. 11.2.1 Preparation of Moisture From the moisture sample prepared from each gross sample, two samples of 1kg each shall be obtained by increment reduction method after mixing the sample on a non-moisture absorbent surface. Alternatively, separate moisture samples may be drawn at the time of collection of gross sample. At least five increments should be taken from each lot and about 20-25 kg of sample must be drawn for each moisture sample. This shall then be crushed down to pass 10 mm IS sieve. From this sample, two or more samples of 1 kg each shall be drawn for moisture sample. These samples shall be sealed in water-tight containers with suitable lid and sent for moisture determination. 11.2.2 Laboratory Samples for Chemical Analysis The laboratory samples shall be obtained after the material is pulverized to pass through 150 micron IS sieve. Each laboratory samples shall be minimum of 150 g. The material so obtained shall be divided into three or more equal parts, as requested by the purchaser, the supplier, the referee and others, if any. All the laboratory samples shall be preserved in dry, clean, and well-stoppered containers and labelled with full identification particulars like, source of the ore, category of the ore, supplier's name, the lot and sub-lot number and date of sampling. If the samples are found to contain sufficient moisture, which hampers crushing and mixing stages during sample preparation they shall be dried at not more than 105oC before any stage of sample preparation, specially during grinding to sizes below 1mm. 11.3 Reduction of Samples One or more of the following method of sample reduction shall be used for dividing a gross sample or a composite sample: a) Riffle division method, b) Coning and quartering method, and c) Increment reduction method. 11.3.1 Riffle Division Method Depending upon the whole-through sieve size of the sample, an appropriate riffle divider specified in Table 6 shall be selected. Table 6 Particle Size of Sample and Size of the Riffle Divider

w1, w2..........wn = mass of the different gross sample excluding the lumps; n = total number of lumps in all the gross samples; and b1, b2 ..........bn = mass of ore in the size range B in different gross samples.
NOTE -- For lumps and sized ores, each lump picked up in the course of sampling is supposed to represent one increment of 8 kg.

11 REDUCTION OF GROSS SAMPLE 11.1 Each of the gross samples shall be first sent for determination of size distribution and only after that sample preparation shall be conducted. However, in the case of gross sample of fines, determination of size distribution may be carried out after reduction of gross sample. The stages of reducing gross sample from each sub-lot for preparing chemical analysis sample and moisture sample are shown in flow chart given at Annex B.
NOTES 1 If it is desired to draw separate moisture samples from each sub-lot, they shall be collected by drawing separate additional increments. Minimum number of increments, in case of fine ores, representing a sub-lot shall also be 20 instead of 10, since fine ore retains comparatively more moisture than lumpy ores. These additional increments shall be combined for each sub-lot and be kept in air-tight containers with full details of sampling before they are sent for moisture sample preparation. 2 When the number of sub-lots constituting a lot is three or less, separate samples shall be drawn from physical tests parallel to the normal samples, so that about 200 kg of composite sample for the lot is available for sample preparation.

11.2 Preparation of Samples for Physical Test, Moisture and Chemical Analysis Each gross sample shall be reduced separately. Ore in each gross sample shall be first crushed in jaw crusher or roll crusher or manually using a hammer and manganese steel plate till all the ore passes 10 mm IS sieve. This shall then be further processed in stages detailed in Annex B to prepare laboratory final sample for chemical analysis and moisture determination. In case separate moisture samples are 7

IS 1449 : 2010 11.3.1.1 Procedure The sample shall be mixed well and placed with a uniform thickness into the riffle tray and divided into almost equal parts by carefully feeding the sample to the riffle uniformly, midway at right angles, across the length of the riffle chutes. Either of the two divided samples shall be selected at random each time the sample is reduced. The division shall be carried out in accordance with Table 7 and the sample shall not be divided further than the mass corresponding to the particle size specified in the table.
NOTES 1 Any material retained in the slots of the riffle shall be removed and added to the respective divided portion of the sample. 2 Samples receivers of the riffler shall properly fit the outlets of the riffle bench and shall be of such design as to ensure prevention of escaping fine particles from the divided parts. 3 Inside surface of the riffle divider shall be flat and smooth. The angle between the inclined surfaces of adjacent chutes shall be 60 o. 4 This method is not applicable to divide samples, containing high moisture content, of sticky iron ores. However, samples may be sufficiently dried before division.

From each of the 20 parts so obtained, equal quantities of the ore shall be collected by use of a suitable scoop once or more number of times depending upon the quantity of divided sample. 11.3.3.1 The method of increment reduction is recommended only when the division ratio is high. As such, in the illustration given in Table 2, this method can be applied in the initial stage when the gross sample is reduced and also at the final stage for obtaining laboratory samples for obtaining duplicate moisture samples. Increment reduction method is preferred to other methods of sample reduction. 11.3.2 Coning and Quartering Method The crushed ore shall be well mixed up and then scooped into a cone-shaped pile. Care should be taken to drop each scoopful exactly over the same spot as otherwise the central axis of the cone will be slackened and an uneven distribution of lumps and the fines will result. After the cone is formed, it shall be flattened by pressing the top of the cone with the smooth surface of the scoop. Then it is cut into quarters by two lines, which intersect at right angles at the centre of the cone. The bulk of the sample is reduced by rejecting any two diagonally opposite quarters. The sample to be divided shall not be more than 12.5 mm as maximum particle size. The division shall be carried out in accordance with Table 7. During the collection of sample, the scoop shall be thrust to the bottom of the sample layer. It is recommended that a flat bumper plate be thrust vertically in the sample layer in front of the scoop during collection. The dimension of the increment scoop to be used for various particle size of the sample is given in Table 9 and Fig. 2. When the mass of the sample divided is expected to be smaller than that required for subsequent procedure, the mass of the increment and/or number of increment shall be increased. 12 NUMBER OF TESTS 12.1 Moisture Sample All the moisture samples representing a lot shall be tested individually for moisture content. Duplicate moisture determinations shall be made for each sublot. To avoid any change in the moisture content, the moisture determination shall be down as quickly as possible, after the sample is taken. 12.2 Sub-lot Laboratory Samples All the sub-lot laboratory samples shall be tested 8

For testing the remaining characteristics, a composite sample as prescribed in 3.1.3 shall be prepared and analyzed. The following scheme is recommended for chemical testing of manganese ore: 9 a) Chemical constitutent of the ore for which sub-lot samples are analyzed individually, Mn and Fe content or any other chemical characteristics which is important or found variable

IS 1449 : 2010 b) Chemical constitutent of the ore for which a composite samples is analyzed, All the radicals stipulated in the contract. 13 REPORTING 13.1 For those characteristics where a composite sample has been tested, only one test result will be available and that result shall be reported as the value of the characteristic for the lot sampled. 13.1.1 When only two laboratory samples have been analyzed individually from a lot, the average of the two available test results shall be reported as the value of the characteristics for the lot sampled. In the case of sub-lots of approximately equal mass, this average shall be calculated as one half of the sum of two test results. If the sub-lots are of varying mass, then the weighted average shall be calculated as the sum of each test result multiplied by corresponding fraction got on dividing the sub-lot weight by the total weight. The individual results shall also be reported to give an indication of the range of variation in quality. 13.1.2 When three or more laboratory samples have been analyzed individually from a lot for any characteristics, the following procedure shall be followed to assess the average quality and its limits of variation: Let x 1, x 2, x 3.... x n be the results of analyzing in laboratory samples for a particular characteristics Calculate x1 + x2 + x3 .......xn if sub-lots are of n approximately equal mass or weighted-average Average ( x ) = (x)= w1x1 + w2x2 + w3x3 .......wnxn w1+ w2+ w3 +..........wn Range (R) = difference between the maximum and minimum of the value of test results (when n is less than 10) or ( R) = the average value of ranges. When the number of sub-lots n is equal to 10 or more, the corresponding results on laboratory samples (10 or more) should be constituted into two groups in the order of their occurrence. For each group, range (R) should be calculated and the average value (R) of the R's should be used in the subsequent clause. The average level of the characteristic in the lot shall be reported is equal to (x). The limits of variation in the average level of the lot shall be reported as (x + hR), where h is a factor, the value of which depends on the number of samples analyzed. The appropriate value of the factor h shall be taken from the following table (with confidence co-efficient of 95 percent): No. of Laboratory Sample Analyzed 3 4 5 6 7 8 10 12 14 16 18 Value of the Factor (h) 1.30 0.72 0.51 0.40 0.33 0.29 0.31 0.25 0.21 0.19 0.17

where w1,w2, w3...., wn are the mass of the sub-lots

NOTE -- The standard deviation of the characteristics shall be calculated for the total number of sub-lots prepared and the value of ` h ' shall be obtained from the Table 5 of IS 1548 (Part 1). In case the number of sublots prepared are different from those of Table 1 and the factor ` h ' cannot be obtained from the table above.

ANNEX A (Clause 5.2)
STOPPED-BELT REFERENCE SAMPLING A-1 Stopped-belt sampling is the accepted method for obtaining a reference sample against which other sampling procedures may be compared. However, special care is required, if the samples are for moisture determination, because moisture may be lost while the reference sample is being removed from the conveyor. The procedure for sampling from a stopped-belt is as follows: Determine the parameters for sampling in accordance with 5; b) Stop the belt at the time or mass intervals determined in accordance with 5; c) At each stoppage, place a suitably profiled sampling frame (see Fig. 3) with minimum internal dimensions of 3 times the nominal top size of the ore or 30 mm, whichever is the greater, across the width of the stationary belt and insert it through the ore so that it is in contact with the belt across its full width; a) d) Should any ore particles obstruct insertion of the sampling frame, push those at the left-hand edge of the frame into the increment and those at the right-hand edge of the frame out of the increment; e) Remove the ore within the sampling frame in the shortest possible time to minimize moisture loss, ensuring that all ore particles are collected by sweeping the belt clean, and deposit each increment into a suitable container; f) If paired comparison are required on an increment-by-increment basis, keep the increments separate; g) If the quality of the lot is required, combine the increments into partial samples or a gross samples in accordance with 5.3; and h) Store the increments, partial samples or gross samples in labelled containers as specified in 4.1.1.
